passages.title: The Inevitable Hour and its awe
passages.tafsir:
The surah opens by naming the Day of Judgement — **al-Ḥāqqah**, "the Inevitable Hour" — and then, instead of describing it, asks about it twice over. Ayah 1 is a single word; ayah 2 asks "What is the Inevitable Hour?"; ayah 3 pushes further: "And what will make you realize what the Inevitable Hour is?" What holds these three ayat together is that movement from a name, to a question, to a question about whether you could even take in the answer. The subject is announced, and the announcement itself is made to feel enormous.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this surah is almost wholly devoted to one theme: the inevitability of the Resurrection, its horrors, the punishment of those who reject it and the reward of those who believe. These opening three ayat are the door into that theme.

## The word al-Ḥāqqah

Ibn Kathir states simply that **al-Ḥāqqah is one of the names of the Day of Judgement**, and he gives the reason for the name: *because during it the promise and the threat will inevitably occur.* Everything Allah has promised and everything He has warned of comes due on that Day. Nothing stays pending. That is what makes the Day "the Inevitable".

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up further, rendering the name "Imminent Happening" and drawing out two senses it carries in Arabic:

- **An established fact, an inevitable event, a reality, a truth.** In this sense the Day of Judgement itself is an established truth and its occurrence is a certainty. It is not a possibility being floated; it is a fact that has not yet arrived.
- **Something that provides evidence that something is true** — something that proves a matter, that makes the real state of things undeniable.

Both senses fit the Day, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies both: in the first sense the Day is itself certain; in the second sense, *the Day of Judgement will prove to the believers the reality of Paradise and to the unbelievers the reality of Hell.* On that Day nothing is any longer a report to be accepted or rejected. What was believed is seen; what was denied is met.

Notice how much is packed into that one word standing alone in ayah 1. It is not "a day is coming"; it is a proper name, spoken as if the hearer already ought to know it — the Certainty, the Thing-That-Proves-True. And the two senses are not really two subjects. A thing so firmly real that it must occur is exactly the kind of thing that, when it occurs, settles every argument about it. The certainty and the proving are one quality of the Day seen from two sides.

## Why a name, then two questions

Ibn Kathir reads the sequence as deliberate: because al-Ḥāqqah means what it means, **"Allah has declared the greatness of this matter"** — and then quotes ayah 3, *"And what will make you know what al-Ḥāqqah is?"*, as the form that declaration takes. The greatness of the Day is not asserted in an adjective. It is conveyed by the shape of the speech itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the effect of the questioning: this name of the Day is followed by two questions about it, and *the questions have been put to make the readers realise how horrifying the experience would be — beyond normal experience or even imagination.*

That last phrase is the key to the passage. A question can do something a description cannot. If Allah had listed the features of that Day here, the mind would have filed them alongside the terrible things it already knows — the worst storm, the worst earthquake, the worst grief. By asking instead, the ayat tell you that your existing stock of experience has nothing in it to measure this by.

The two questions are also not the same question asked twice. Ayah 2 asks what it is. Ayah 3 asks what could possibly *make you know* what it is — which is a question about the reach of your knowing, not about the Day. It implies that no ordinary means of knowledge arrives at this. The knowledge has to come from Allah's own telling, which is exactly what the rest of the surah then supplies.

So the passage does something unusual: it makes the reader's inability part of the message. You are not being handed a fact to file away. You are being told, before anything is described, that the reality outruns you.

## Where the passage is heading

Ibn Kathir marks the turn that follows with a single line: **"Then Allah mentions the destruction of the nations that denied the Resurrection."** The surah will not answer its own question with a definition; it will turn to history, to what happened to those who rejected the Day. But that answer belongs to the ayat after these. What ayat 1–3 do is hold the reader at the threshold — named, questioned, and made to feel small before the telling begins.

## Living it

**Take the certainty seriously.** The first thing these ayat ask is not fear but conviction. Ibn Kathir's reason for the name — that on that Day the promise and the threat inevitably occur — is a statement about Allah's truthfulness, not merely about the future. A person who genuinely holds that everything Allah promised will come due cannot treat his own deeds as weightless.

**Do not domesticate the Day.** Ayah 3 signals that the reality is beyond normal experience and imagination, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it. So the honest response to the question "What is al-Ḥāqqah?" is not a confident summary but a stilled heart. Familiarity with the words of a surah can quietly shrink what they point to; the questions in ayat 2 and 3 exist precisely to stop that from happening.

**Let the coming warning do its work.** Ibn Kathir's framing of what follows — "the nations that denied the Resurrection" and their destruction — ties denial and ruin into a single story. It is set down for a reader who still has time, which is the whole reason such an account is told rather than merely recorded.

**Prepare to be proved right or proved wrong.** In the second sense Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives, al-Ḥāqqah is the day that proves the truth: Paradise made real for the believers, Hell made real for the deniers. If that is what the Day does, then every day before it is a day in which what a person will meet there is still being settled.

passages.title: Thamud and 'Ad destroyed for denial
passages.tafsir:
These ayat take the Day whose name has just been announced — **al-Ḥāqqah** — and show what happened to two nations who called it a lie. The link that holds the passage together is simple and devastating: they denied a Striking, and a striking came for them; and ayah 8 closes the file with a question no one can answer.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this surah is almost wholly devoted to one subject: the inevitability of the Resurrection, its horrors, the punishment of unbelievers and the reward of believers. It observes that the Day of Judgment is referred to by various names in the Qurʼān, and that three of them appear in this surah: **al-Ḥāqqah** ("Imminent Happening"), **al-Qāriʿah** ("Shocking Event"), and **al-Wāqiʿah** ("Happening").

Ibn Kathīr explains that *al-Ḥāqqah* is one of the names of the Day of Judgement "because during it the promise and the threat will inevitably occur" — everything Allah has promised and everything He has warned of comes true on that Day, with nothing left pending. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second layer to the word: *al-ḥāqqah* means an established fact, an inevitable event, a reality or truth; and it also means something that *provides evidence* that something is true. Both senses apply, it says: the Day is itself an established truth whose occurrence is a certainty, and it is the Day that will prove to the believers the reality of Paradise and to the unbelievers the reality of Hell.

Ayat 1–3 asked twice over — *What is al-Ḥāqqah? And what will make you know what al-Ḥāqqah is?* — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: the questions are put "to make the readers realise how horrifying the experience would be — beyond normal experience or even imagination." Then, at ayah 4, Allah stops describing and starts pointing. Ibn Kathīr titles this section plainly: *Mention of the Destruction of the Nations* — "Then Allah mentions the destruction of the nations that denied the Resurrection."

## Ayah 4: the word they called a lie

> **˹Both˺ Thamūd and ʿĀd denied the Striking Disaster.**

The verb is *kadhdhabat* — they declared it false, called it a lie. And what they called a lie is named here not as al-Ḥāqqah but as **al-Qāriʿah**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *al-Qāriʿah* literally means "rumbling," and that the Day is so called "because there will be rumbling sound which will cause agitation or terror in the hearts of people, and will dreadfully destroy the heavenly and earthly bodies and scatter them apart."

Hold on to that: a **sound** that terrifies hearts and pulls the heavens and the earth apart. That is what these two nations said would never come. Now read ayat 5 and 6 and notice what Allah sent them.

Notice too that ayah 4 puts them together — Thamūd first, then ʿĀd — under one verdict, and only then separates them in ayat 5 and 6 with *fa-ammā… wa-ammā…* ("as for… and as for…"). One shared denial; two distinct punishments.

## Ayah 5: Thamūd and *aṭ-Ṭāghiyah*

> **As for Thamūd, they were destroyed by an overwhelming blast.**

*Aṭ-Ṭāghiyah* is one of those Qurʼānic words a translation can only gesture at. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to the root *ṭughyān*, which means "to exceed the limit," and says the word signifies an extremely severe punishment: "it would be such high pitched sound which would exceed the limit of any of the sounds of the mortal world, and the human heart or brain would not be able to bear." It describes the punishment as a combination of the most high-pitched sound of a thunderbolt together with a flash of lightning that struck them and rent their hearts.

Then comes the sentence that unlocks the whole ayah: **"When Thamūd exceeded the limit in denying the Day of Judgment, they were destroyed by that dreadful cry which exceeded all limits."** Their denial exceeded bounds, and the punishment that answered it exceeded bounds. The word for the crime became the word for the sentence.

Ibn Kathīr reports the two readings the early scholars gave the word:

- **The punishment itself.** Ibn Kathīr says it is "the cry which will silence them, and the quake that will silence them," and Qatādah said something similar: "*Aṭ-Ṭāghiyah* is the shout."
- **Their own transgression.** Mujāhid said "*Aṭ-Ṭāghiyah* means the sins," and this was also said by ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and Ibn Zayd, who said that it means transgression. Ibn Zayd then recited as proof: *Thamūd denied through their transgression* (91:11).

Both readings are reported from the early authorities, and Ibn Kathīr passes them on side by side without discarding either. The transgression and the blast that answered it are, in the end, one story told from its two ends.

## Ayah 6: ʿĀd and a wind stripped of mercy

> **And as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind.**

Two adjectives carry this ayah, and they pull in different directions.

**Ṣarṣar.** Ibn Kathīr glosses it simply: "a cold wind." Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same — "This means cold." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the two qualities together: *rīḥin ṣarṣarin* refers to a violent windstorm which is also severely cold.

**ʿĀtiyah.** Qatādah, as-Suddī, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and ath-Thawrī all said this means severe blowing of the wind. Qatādah described it vividly: "It blew fiercely upon them until it pierced their hearts." Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk added the dimension that should stop us: it blew fiercely upon them "without any mercy or blessing."

That last phrase is worth sitting with. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk's wording carries a quiet assumption — that mercy and blessing are what a wind would ordinarily bring with it — and it tells us this wind came stripped of both. ʿAlī and others said it blew fiercely upon their stored harvest until it was brought out worthless: even what they had put away and secured was turned to nothing.

Ibn Kathīr notes that it has been confirmed in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"I was helped by an easterly wind and the people of ʿĀd were destroyed by a westerly wind."**

The same created thing — moving air — is help for one people and destruction for another. Nothing in creation acts on its own account.

## Ayah 7: seven nights and eight days, in succession

> **Which Allah imposed on them for seven nights and eight days Ḥusūm, so that you could see men lying toppled, as if they were trunks of date palms, Khāwiyah!**

The verb is *sakhkharahā* — Ibn Kathīr explains it as "He made it overpower them." The wind did not merely arise; it was imposed upon them and made to overpower them.

**Ḥusūman.** Ibn Kathīr gives the range of meaning: "complete, successive and unfortunately evil." Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ath-Thawrī and others all said it means **in succession** — one after another, with no break. It is reported that ʿIkrimah and ar-Rabīʿ bin Khuthaym both said it means it was **unfortunately evil upon them**, which Ibn Kathīr likens to Allah's words *in days of calamity* (41:16).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word from its root: *ḥusūman* is the plural of *ḥāsim*, and means "cutting them off entirely" or "causing them to perish completely."

On the counting, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to some of the narratives the windstorm began on a Wednesday morning and lasted until the following Wednesday evening, which in this way makes up eight days and seven nights.

**"As if they were trunks of date palms."** Then the ayah pulls back and shows the aftermath: *fa-tara l-qawma fīhā ṣarʿā* — "so that you could see the people lying toppled." Of *khāwiyah*, Ibn ʿAbbās said it means **ruined**; others besides him said it means **dilapidated**. Ibn Kathīr spells out the picture: the wind would cause a palm tree to hit the ground, and it would fall down dead on a man's head; then his head would shatter, and he would remain a lifeless corpse, as if it were without branches, motionless.

That last phrase carries the force of the comparison. Not a person struck down, but a thing left lying — stripped, still, indistinguishable from fallen wood.

## Ayah 8: the question with no answer

> **Do you see any of them left alive?**

*Fa-hal tarā lahum min bāqiyah.* Ibn Kathīr reads the question as put to anyone who cares to look: do you find any one of them left, "or anyone who even attributes himself to being from them?" Not a survivor. Not a descendant. Not even someone who *claims* the lineage. "Rather they are all gone, right down to the last of them, and Allah did not make for them any successors."

This is why the passage ends in a question rather than a statement. A statement would ask you to believe a report; a question hands you the evidence and lets the silence answer.

## What the passage is arguing

Read as a unit, ayat 4–8 are not a history lesson but a proof. Ibn Kathīr's framing is the key: these are "the nations that denied the Resurrection." The Qurʼān's reply to that denial is not abstract. It says, in effect: you doubt that a Striking can come? Two peoples said exactly that, and a striking came for them inside history.

And notice how closely each punishment resembles the thing that was denied. Al-Qāriʿah, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it, is a rumbling sound that fills hearts with terror and tears apart the bodies of the heavens and the earth. Thamūd, who denied it, were taken by a cry that "exceeded all limits" and rent their hearts. ʿĀd were taken by a wind that pierced their hearts and left men lying toppled on the ground. They denied a sound; a sound and a wind came for them.

Then ayah 8 puts the result where no one can argue with it. The nations who said the Striking would never arrive are the ones with no one left to say it — not a survivor, not a descendant, not even a claimant to the name.

## Living it

**Take the excess seriously.** *Ṭughyān*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, means going past the limit. Its reading of ayah 5 — that Thamūd "exceeded the limit in denying," and so met what "exceeded all limits" — is a warning about a posture, not merely about an event. It is denial pushed past its bounds that invites the answer.

**Do not mistake a blessing for a guarantee.** ʿĀd were felled by wind, blowing this time "without any mercy or blessing," as aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk put it — and even their stored harvest, ʿAlī said, was brought out worthless. The same moving air, as the Prophet ﷺ said, was help for him and destruction for a nation. Nothing in creation is inherently on our side; it does what Allah makes it do.

**Let ayah 8 do its work.** *Do you see any of them left alive?* The question is put to the reader, not to Thamūd. It asks whether we will draw the conclusion or read past it — whether, when the reminder comes, ours will be the kind of hearing that keeps what it hears.

passages.title: Pharaoh, the overturned cities, and the Ark
passages.tafsir:
Ayat 9–12 close the surah's roll-call of ruined nations and then turn it inside out. Allah names Pharaoh, those reckoned with him, and the overturned cities — all convicted of the same single offence and all seized by the same punishment. Then, in ayah 11, the direction reverses: instead of one more drowning we are shown a rescue, and told that *we* are the ones who were carried. That is what holds these four ayat together: those who denied their Messengers were seized, and every human being alive to hear this is descended from the handful who were saved.

Ibn Kathir places this whole sequence under a single heading — "Mention of the Destruction of the Nations" — and explains that Allah is mentioning "the destruction of the nations that denied the Resurrection." So this is not history recounted for its own sake. Every name is evidence in a case about the Last Day.

## Ayah 9: three defendants, one charge

**"Pharaoh, and those before him."** Ibn Kathir records that the Arabic *wa man qablahu* has been recited in two ways, and each opens a slightly different shade of meaning. Recited with a *kasrah* (the short vowel *i*) under the letter *qāf* — *qibalahu* — the meaning changes to "those who were with him in his time, and they were his followers who were disbelieving Coptic people." Recited with a *fatḥah* (the short vowel *a*) over the *qāf* — *qablahu* — it means "those nations before him who were similar to him."

Neither reading cancels the other; between them they say that Pharaoh was neither the first of his kind nor alone in his kind. Tyranny has ancestors, and it has staff.

**"And the overturned cities."** *Al-muʾtafikāt* is the hardest word in the passage, and the two commentaries come at it from different angles.

Ibn Kathir keeps the identification broad: the overthrown cities are "those nations that rejected their Messengers."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān narrows and explains. The word, it says, means *adjacent to one another*, and it refers to the towns of Sayyidnā Lūṭ — Sodom and Gomorrah — either because they were adjacent to each other, or because when the punishment overtook the disbelievers and criminals, overthrowing their towns, they were all jumbled up together. Muftī Muhammad Taqi Usmani adds in a note that "another possible meaning of *muʾtafikāt* is 'overthrown' as mentioned by several exegetes," and that is the sense his translation follows.

Hold both pictures at once and you feel the word. A cluster of settlements sitting side by side — and then the whole cluster upended, everything jumbled into rubble. The Qurʾān does not name these towns here at all. It identifies them by what happened to them.

**"Committed *al-khāṭiʾah*."** Ibn Kathir identifies the offence precisely: *al-khāṭiʾah* "means their rejection of what Allah revealed." Two other early authorities put it differently — Ar-Rabīʿ said it means disobedience; Mujāhid said, "They committed errors."

Put the readings together and the shape of the charge appears. Pharaoh's crime and the crime of the overturned cities were not, at bottom, two different crimes. Whatever the surface behaviour, what they held in common was this: revelation came, and they turned it away.

## Ayah 10: one Messenger, all the Messengers

*Fa-ʿaṣaw rasūla rabbihim* — "and they disobeyed their Lord's Messenger." The singular is deliberate, and Ibn Kathir stops on it: it means "they were all of the same type, they all denied the Messenger of Allah who was sent to them." Different centuries, different lands, different Prophets — one identical act, repeated.

He then cites Allah's word, "Everyone of them denied the Messengers, so My threat took effect," and draws out something larger: "So whoever denies a Messenger, then verily, he denies all of the Messengers." His proof is the Qurʾān's own way of speaking. Allah says of Nūḥ's people that they *belied the Messengers* (26:105), of ʿĀd that they *belied the Messengers* (26:123), of Thamūd that they *belied the Messengers* (26:141) — plural every time — "however, only one Messenger came to every nation."

Each people rejected exactly one man; the Qurʾān records it as rejecting them all. What they were really refusing was not a personality but the fact of being addressed by their Lord. Refuse that once and you have refused it everywhere.

Notice too the phrasing the ayah chooses: not merely "a messenger" but *their Lord's Messenger* — *rasūla rabbihim*. The messenger they threw back belonged to the very Lord they were disobeying. The wording makes the ingratitude audible.

**The seizure.** *Fa-akhadhahum akhdhatan rābiyah* — "so He seized them with a punishment that was *rābiyah*." Ibn Kathir glosses *rābiyah*: it "means, great, severe and painful." Mujāhid said, "*Rābiyah* means severe." As-Suddī said, "It means destructive."

Three witnesses, three angles on one word: great in scale, severe in force, destructive in outcome. Nothing survived it.

## Ayah 11: the water that rose beyond its limits

Now the passage turns. *Innā lammā ṭaghā al-māʾ ḥamalnākum fī al-jāriyah* — "Verily, when the water rose beyond its limits, We carried you in the ship."

**What happened.** Ibn Kathir explains that the water "rose up over its shores by the leave of Allah and it overcame all that existed." Ibn ʿAbbās and others said, "The water rising beyond its boundary means it increased abundantly." Two things there are worth sitting with. The flood was total — it overcame all that existed. And it happened *by the leave of Allah*: water does not decide to drown a world.

**Why it happened.** This, Ibn Kathir says, "happened due to the supplication of Nūḥ against his people when they denied him, opposed him and worshipped other than Allah. Therefore, Allah answered his supplication and the people of the earth were covered with the flood except for those who were with Nūḥ in the ship."

**"We carried *you*."** Here is the hinge of the whole passage. Allah does not say "We carried them." He says *ḥamalnākum* — **We carried you**, addressing people born long after the water receded. Ibn Kathir supplies the reason: "Thus, are humans all from the loins of Nūḥ and his progeny. For this reason Allah reminds humanity of His blessing."

So every listener has a place in that ship. On Ibn Kathir's reading, your existence is a survivor's existence — you were present at a rescue, in the loins of an ancestor, when the alternative was that your line ended in the water.

**"In *al-jāriyah*."** Ibn Kathir glosses the word simply: "a ship running along upon the surface of the water." It is a picture of motion. While everything that existed was overcome, this one thing kept running along on top.

## Ayah 12: a sign that still sails, and an ear that keeps it

*Li-najʿalahā lakum tadhkiratan* — "That We might make it an admonition for you."

**What does "it" refer to?** Ibn Kathir gives his own reading first: the pronoun "it" here "refers to the species of the object (ships) due to the general meaning alluding to this." The meaning is then: "We caused its type of creation (ships) to remain (in the earth) for you, so that you ride upon the currents of the water in the seas."

He then reports a second view, from Qatādah: "Allah caused this ship to remain until the first people of this Ummah saw it" — the vessel of Nūḥ itself, preserved as a monument. Ibn Kathir does not leave the choice open: "However, the first view (that it refers to all ships in general) is the most apparent."

He grounds his reading in the Qurʾān's own habit of pointing at ships as signs: *and has appointed for you ships and cattle on which you ride; in order that you may mount on their backs, and then may remember the favour of your Lord when you mount thereon* (43:12–13); and *And an Āyah for them is that We bore their offspring in the laden ship. And We have created for them of the like thereunto, on which they ride* (36:41–42).

That is quietly magnificent. On this reading the reminder was not left as a single relic to be visited. It was built into the ordinary furniture of human life: a kind of creation kept in place on the earth so that people would go on riding the water and go on remembering who put them safely on top of it.

**"And that it might be retained by the retaining ears."** *Wa taʿiyahā udhun wāʿiyah.* Ibn Kathir's summary is that this means "a receptive ear may understand and reflect upon this bounty," and he gathers the early explanations:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "This means an ear that is retentive and hearing."
- **Qatādah**: "An ear that Allah gives intelligence, so it benefits by what it hears from Allah's Book."
- **Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk**: "An ear that hears it and retains it, meaning the person who has sound hearing, and correct intellect."

And Ibn Kathir closes the door on any narrowing: "And this is general concerning everyone who understands and retains." The description is a standing invitation, not a private title held by a few.

So the ayah ends with two things that hold: a ship that holds people above the water, and an ear that holds meaning inside a person.

## Living it

**Recognise which side of the water you are on.** Ayah 11 has already assigned you a role: not spectator, but survivor. If all humans are from the loins of Nūḥ, as Ibn Kathir says, then Allah's "We carried you" is addressed to you directly. What it asks for is not curiosity about ancient shipbuilding but gratitude that knows whose it is.

**Let ordinary things work as signs.** On Ibn Kathir's preferred reading, the reminder is not in a museum; it is in every vessel that carries people across water. And the Qurʾān he cites is explicit about the mechanism: you mount, and then you remember your Lord's favour (43:13). The remembering is the point of the riding.

**Aim to be the retaining ear.** In Qatādah's wording, this is an ear "that Allah gives intelligence" — a gift to ask Him for, not merely a technique to practise. In Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk's, it involves hearing *and* holding: sound hearing together with correct intellect. Reading these ayat and retaining nothing an hour later is exactly the gap the last words of the passage address. The nations of ayat 9–10 were not deaf. As Ibn Kathir defines their offence, *al-khāṭiʾah* was "their rejection of what Allah revealed" — revelation reached them, and they turned it away. The ayah's closing prayer is for the opposite: an ear that receives it, and keeps it.

passages.title: The Trumpet, cosmic collapse, and judgment
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are a single unbroken scene: the sound that ends the world, the collapse of everything solid above and beneath us, and then — with the wreckage cleared away — human beings standing exposed before their Lord. In *Tafsir Ibn Kathir* the passage runs under the heading "A Mention of the Horrors of the Day of Judgement," and Ibn Kathir opens by saying that Allah informs us here of the horrors that will take place on that Day. What holds the ayat together is a chain of "and then… and then…" that never pauses for breath. The destination of the whole sequence is ayah 18: *you* will be brought forward, and nothing about you will stay hidden.

## Ayah 13: one blast, and that is enough

**What the Trumpet is.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Tirmidhi records a hadith on the authority of Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the *ṣūr* — the "Trumpet" — is a horn-like object which will be blown on Doomsday. It is a real thing, not a figure of speech.

**"One blast" — نَفۡخَةٞ وَٰحِدَةٞ.** Ibn Kathir draws the whole meaning out of that single word *wāḥidah*, "one": it is emphasised here that it is one blowing "because the command of Allah cannot be opposed or prevented, and it does not need to be repeated or stressed." Think of how human commands work. An order has to be repeated because it might be ignored, resisted, or missed. Allah's command has no such weakness. One breath into the horn, and it is done — with no second call needed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a different shade to the same word: it means "a sudden and a single continuing sound that will last until all die" — not a short note, but one unbroken sound stretching over the dying of everything alive.

## How many blasts are there?

The sources give this real attention, and it is worth following carefully.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** says the texts of Qur'an and Sunnah show the Trumpet will be blown twice on the Day of Judgment:

- **Nafkhat-us-ṣaʿaq**, "the trumpet of swoon." The Qur'an says of it, *"And all those in the heavens and all those in the earth will faint…"* (39:68). With this trumpet all the angels residing in the heavens, and all the jinn, human beings and animals residing on earth, will become unconscious and fall to the ground; and while they are in that state of unconsciousness, they will die.
- **Nafkhat-ul-baʿth**, "the trumpet of Resurrection" — the word *baʿth* meaning "to rise." With this trumpet all the dead will rise from death and stand up. The Qur'an describes it: *"Thereafter, it will be blown once again, and suddenly they will stand up, looking around"* (39:68).

According to some narratives, a third trumpet will also be blown before these two, **nafkhat-ul-fazaʿ**, "the trumpet of fright or panic." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a reconciliation, referring it to a work it cites simply as *Mazhari* (the bundle before us gives no more than the name): by a careful analysis of all the narratives and texts, it appears that the first trumpet in its *initial* stage is the blast of fright, and in its *final* stage becomes *ṣaʿaq*, the blast of swoon or death. In other words, one continuous sounding with two effects — first panic, then collapse and death — which fits closely with "a single continuing sound that will last until all die."

**Ibn Kathir** lists these events in this order: the first is the blowing of fright, which will be followed by the blowing of destruction, "when everyone in the heavens and the earth will be struck down except whoever Allah wills"; then, after this, the blowing of standing before the Lord of all that exists, and the resurrection, and the gathering. Of that last one he says: "And this is that blowing." Either way, the passage is standing at the hinge between the two worlds.

## Ayah 14: the earth carried, then flattened

*"And the earth and the mountains shall be removed from their places, and crushed with a single crushing."*

Two verbs, and both are strange to the imagination. First the earth and the mountains are **carried** — lifted up, handled like an object that can be picked up, removed from their places. Then they are crushed.

And again that word: **دَكَّةٗ وَٰحِدَةٗ**, "a *single* crushing." The Qur'an insists on it a second time, one ayah after insisting on a single blast. Nothing here requires a second strike.

Ibn Kathir explains the result: "they will be stretched out to the extent of the surface (of the earth) and the earth will change into something else other than the earth." The mountains are not merely knocked down; the terrain is ironed out flat, and the earth becomes a different earth. Hold that image — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān returns to it at ayah 18 and shows why it matters for you personally.

## Ayah 15: the Event falls

*"On that Day the Inevitable Event will have come to pass."*

Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and exact: **al-Wāqiʿah**, "the Event," means the Day of Judgement. After the sound and the crushing, the Qur'an simply states that the Event has occurred.

## Ayah 16: a sky worn thin

*"The sky will then be so torn that it will be frail."*

Rendered by Ibn Kathir's translator as "rent asunder, for that Day it will be frail and torn up." The sky, the most solid-seeming thing above us, is on that Day described as frail.

**Ibn Jurayj** said that this is like Allah's statement *"And the heaven shall be opened, it will become as gates"* (78:19).

**Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It (the sky) will be torn apart and the Throne will be near it." Sit with that. The ceiling of this world gives way, and in what Ibn ʿAbbās describes, the Throne of the Lord is near.

## Ayah 17: angels on the rim, and eight beneath the Throne

*"with the angels on its sides. On that Day eight ˹mighty angels˺ will bear the Throne of your Lord above them."*

**"The angel" meaning all angels.** Ibn Kathir clarifies that the word *malak* here is referring to the species of angels — all of them; the meaning is that the angels collectively will be standing on the sides of the heavens. **Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas** said of this: they will be standing on what has been ground to powder of the heavens, looking at the people of the earth.

Put the scene together as the sources describe it. Below: an earth stretched out flat and changed into something other than the earth. Above: the heavens rent asunder. Ranged around the sides: the angels, looking at the people of the earth. There is nowhere on that ground that is not overlooked.

**The eight.** Ibn Kathir: this means that on the Day of Judgement eight angels will carry the Throne. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that according to some of the Prophetic narratives, before the Judgment Day this task will be carried out by four angels, and on the Judgment Day four more angels will be added to carry out the task.

**How large are they?** Abu Dawud recorded from Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was permitted to speak about one of the angels among those angels who carry the Throne of Allah. Between the lobe of his ear to his shoulder is the distance of seven hundred years (of travelling)." Ibn Kathir notes that this is the wording recorded in Abu Dawud. Sit with the measurement for a moment. Not his height — the span of one side of his neck. And he is one of eight, and the eight are carrying something.

**"Your Lord" — رَبِّكَ.** In the middle of this vastness the address turns personal, spoken to the Prophet ﷺ: the Throne of *your* Lord. The One whose Throne eight such bearers carry is the same One who is your Lord.

## What we affirm about the Throne — and where we stop

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here to lay down a rule of belief. As to what the Throne of the Raḥmān is, what its reality, its form and shape are, and how the angels carry it — these are transcendental matters and are all beyond human intellect. Allah is beyond time, space and matter, and therefore we are not permitted to pursue these matters pertaining to Him to determine their exact meaning. The noble Companions, their pupils and the righteous elders took the attitude that they simply believed in all such transcendental matters and never questioned about them. Whatever Allah means by them is the Truth; their nature and reality are unknown.

So we affirm the Throne, and we affirm that eight angels bear it on that Day, exactly as Allah has said — without inventing a picture of it, and without explaining the words away into metaphor. Neither denial nor imagination; affirmation with restraint. Imitating the early generations on this point is itself part of the benefit of the passage.

## Ayah 18: presented, with nothing hidden

*"You will then be presented ˹before Him for judgment˺, and none of your secrets will stay hidden."*

Everything before this was scenery. This ayah is about you, and the address is direct — Ibn Kathir renders it "you will all be presented."

**تُعۡرَضُونَ** *(tuʿraḍūn)*, rendered "you will be presented," "you will be brought," is passive in every translation before us: no one presents himself; you are brought forward. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "you will all be presented to the Knower of the secrets and private counsels. He is the One from Whom none of your affairs are hidden. He is the Knower of all things apparent, secret and hidden." And that, he says, is the reason Allah goes on to say **لَا تَخۡفَىٰ مِنكُمۡ خَافِيَةٞ** — "not a secret of you will be hidden."

**Why say it here, of all places?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a fine observation. Nothing is concealed from Divine knowledge and sight even today — so why is the Plain of Gathering particularly mentioned in this connection? Probably, it says, because the entire ground will be levelled out as a plain surface. There will be no caves nor mountains, no buildings nor houses nor barriers of any trees. These are the things behind which people normally hide in the mortal world. On the Day of Judgment none of these things will be available, and there will be no possibility of hiding. That is ayah 14 coming back to meet you: the earth stretched out flat, and nothing left to step behind.

**The three presentations.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Mūsā that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people will be exhibited three times on the Day of Judgement. The first two presentations will be (their) arguing and offering excuses. During the third presentation the pages (records) will fly into their hands. Some of them will receive the records in their right hands and some will receive them in their left hands." Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Majah and At-Tirmidhi both recorded this hadith.

Notice the shape of that. Two rounds of what human beings always do when caught — protest and explain. Then the arguing stops, the records arrive, and which hand they land in settles everything.

## Living it

**Take the "one" seriously.** Twice, in ayat 13 and 14, the Qur'an insists on a single blast and a single crushing. Ibn Kathir's reason for the first — that the command of Allah cannot be opposed or prevented, and does not need to be repeated or stressed — is a cure for a specific disease of the heart: the quiet assumption that this Day is far off, negotiable, or somehow avoidable. It arrives the way a command arrives, once.

**Live in front of ayah 18.** The most practical line in this passage is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's: caves, mountains, buildings, houses and trees are what people hide behind in this world, and on that Day there are none. The private sin, the hidden intention behind a public good deed, the version of yourself only you know about — all of it is already known to the Knower of all things apparent, secret and hidden, and on that Day there will be no possibility of hiding. The believer's response is not despair but repentance now, while concealment still has a door: turn back, put right what can be put right, and work on the inward self as carefully as the outward one.

**And remember the words of ayah 17.** In a scene of rent heavens and angels of unimaginable size, Allah calls Himself *your Lord*. The One before whom you will be presented is the One who has been sustaining you all along. That is what makes the terror of this passage bearable, and what makes turning to Him now the only sensible move.

passages.title: The record in the right hand
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat follow one person through the most exposed moment a human being will ever face — the handing over of the record of his life — and show that for him it turns out to be a moment of joy so large he cannot keep it to himself. What holds the passage together is a single grammatical thread: ayah 19 opens with **fa-ammā**, "as for the one who...", and everything that follows — his shout, his explanation, his life of ease, his Garden, his fruit, and the invitation to eat and drink — hangs from that one opening as its consequence. It is one man's story told from the first second of his verdict to his first meal in Paradise.

## Ayah 19: the man who wants everyone to read his file

Ibn Kathir opens his comment simply: Allah is informing us here of **the happiness** of those who receive their Book in the right hand on the Day of Judgement, and of their being pleased with this. And then he notices something about the way that happiness behaves. It does not stay private. "Out of his extreme pleasure," he writes, is his saying this **to everyone that he meets**.

That is the picture. A man walking through the crowds of that Day with a document in his hand, stopping people, pressing it on them: *read it.*

Ibn Kathir explains why he is willing to do this: "He will say this because he knows that what is in it is good and purely virtuous deeds." And then he adds a line that changes the whole scene — this man "will be of those whom Allah replaced their bad deeds (evils) with good deeds." So the file he is so eager to publish is not the file of someone who never slipped. It is a file that has been *dealt with*. What was ugly in it is no longer there to be found.

## The word هَاؤُمُ — a shout, not a sentence

Everything about ayah 19 turns on a word that English cannot really carry: **hā'umu** (هَاؤُمُ).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word *hā'umu* literally means "come", but that idiomatically it is used in the sense of the plural imperative verb **khudhū** — "take". So the shout is roughly: *Here — take it! Read my book!* Ibn Kathir gives the same sense: "take my Book and read it."

Then there is the odd little ending, **-um**. Ibn Kathir reports that 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd said the meaning of the ayah is "Here, read my Book," and that "The suffix '*Um*' is a grammatical addition." Ibn Kathir records that view as his, and then, with characteristic care, adds his own reading: "It seems apparent that the suffix '*Um*' means here **'you all**.'"

That is a small grammatical remark with an enormous consequence for the scene. If the *-um* means "you all", then this man is not handing his record to one person. He is addressing a crowd. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paints exactly that: he "will be elated and, **looking at the people around him**, will say 'Here, take my account book and read it!'"

Hold that against the instinct every honest person knows in this life — the instinct to keep the record of yourself unseen. On that Day, one man will have the opposite instinct. His deepest desire will be for his file to be read aloud.

## Why he is not ashamed: the covering that came first

The sources are careful not to let us imagine that this confidence comes from a spotless life. Two reports in Ibn Kathir explain where it actually comes from.

The first is recorded by **Ibn Abi Hatim** from 'Abdullah bin 'Abdullah bin Hanzalah — Hanzalah being, as Ibn Kathir notes, the Companion who was washed by the angels for his funeral. He said: "Verily, Allah will stop His servant on the Day of Judgement and He will make his sins appear on the outside of his Book of Records. Then He will say to him, 'Did you do this?' The servant will respond, 'Yes my Lord.' Then Allah will say to him, 'I will not expose you (or dishonor you) for it, for verily, I have forgiven you.' The person will then say, '**Here (you all) read my Book!**'"

Notice the sequence. The sins are on the *outside* of the file — the first thing visible, unavoidable. The servant admits them; he does not argue. Only after the admission comes the forgiveness. And only after the forgiveness does the shout of ayah 19 leave his mouth. His confidence is not innocence. It is the confidence of a debt that has just been cancelled in front of him.

The second report Ibn Kathir cites concerns **the private counsel** — the private exchange between Allah and His servant on that Day. The bundle records it as being **"In the Sahih"**, from **Ibn 'Umar**, who was asked about the private counsel and said he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

> "Allah will bring the servant close (to Him) on the Day of Judgement and make him confess all of his sins. This will continue until the servant thinks that he is about to be destroyed. Then Allah will say, 'Verily, I have concealed these sins for you in the worldly life and I have forgiven you for them today.' Then he will be given **his Book of good deeds in his right hand**."

The same hadith then turns to the other side: "about the disbeliever and the hypocrite, the witnesses will say, *'These are those who lied on their Lord, and verily, the curse of Allah is on the wrongdoers.'*" One case is settled quietly, in private, and ends with a book in the right hand. The other is announced publicly by witnesses.

Read the two together and the emotional logic of ayah 19 becomes clear. The man goes through the worst moments of his life one by one, in a closeness he cannot escape, until he is certain he is finished — and then hears that he was covered all along in this world and is forgiven today. A man who has just lived through that would *of course* want the crowd to read what is left.

## Ayah 20: "I was certain I would meet my reckoning"

The believer explains himself in ayah 20. The ayah is rendered in our sources two ways that are worth putting side by side: **"I surely knew I would face my reckoning"**, and, in Ibn Kathir's wording, **"Surely, I did believe that I shall meet my account!"**

That second rendering could be misread as something soft — a hopeful opinion, a probability. Ibn Kathir shuts that door. He states the meaning plainly: "I used to be **certain** in the worldly life that this day would definitely come." And he anchors that reading not in preference but in the Qur'an's own usage, quoting 2:46 — *"(They are those) who are certain that they are going to meet their Lord."* Same expression, and unmistakably certainty.

This is the hinge of the whole passage, and it is worth pausing on. The one thing the man offers as the explanation for his outcome is not a list of achievements. It is a *conviction he carried while he was alive* — that this meeting was real and was coming. Everything in his file grew out of that conviction. Ibn Kathir places ayah 20 exactly where the rescue lands: this, he says, will be "when he (the servant of Allah) will be saved from being disgraced and exposed on the Day of Judgement."

## Ayat 21–23: what such a person walks into

Now the consequences arrive, three at a time.

**"So he shall be in a life, well-pleasing" (21).** The phrase is *ʿīshatin rāḍiyah* — a life that is itself described as *pleased*, an unusual and beautiful way to speak of a life. Ibn Kathir glosses it with one word: **pleasant**.

**"In a lofty Paradise" (22).** *Jannatin ʿāliyah.* Ibn Kathir unpacks it as "having elevated castles, beautiful wide-eyed maidens, pleasant stations and eternal joy." And on the word "lofty" he brings a hadith that gives the scale — confirmed in the Sahih, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Verily, Paradise has one hundred levels and between each level is a distance like the distance between the earth and the sky."* "Lofty" is not decoration. There is real height there, and real distance between one station and another.

**"Whose fruit will hang within reach" (23).** *Quṭūfuhā dāniyah.* Al-Bara' bin 'Azib explained the phrase this way: "This means close enough for one of them (the people of Paradise) to reach them while he is **lying on his bed**." Ibn Kathir adds that more than one person has said this.

Feel the contrast the ayah is drawing. Every fruit in this world sits at the far end of labour — the climbing, the reaching, the waiting for a season. There, the fruit comes to the level of a man who is not even sitting up. Height in ayah 22, nearness in ayah 23: the place is exalted, and yet nothing in it is out of reach.

## Ayah 24: "for what you sent ahead"

Then the address changes. Through ayat 19–23 we have been watching a man from the outside; in ayah 24 he is spoken to directly, and in the plural: **"Eat and drink at ease for that which you have sent on before you in days past."**

Ibn Kathir tells us what kind of speech this is: "this will be said to them as an **invitation** to them of blessing, favor and goodness." Not a wage counted out at a counter — a host welcoming guests to a table.

The word for the deeds is *aslaftum*, "what you have sent on before you" — the image is of something dispatched in advance, arriving ahead of the traveller. And they were sent in **al-ayyām al-khāliyah**, "days past", days that are gone. Every one of those ordinary, forgettable days was a parcel sent forward. They are all waiting here.

## The line Ibn Kathir places right at this point

There is an obvious question in ayah 24, and Ibn Kathir does not dodge it. If the Garden is *"for that which you have sent on before"*, is Paradise then purchased by deeds? He answers by placing, right here, a hadith confirmed in the Sahih, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Work deeds, strive, seek to draw near (to Allah) and know that **none of you will be admitted into Paradise because of his deeds**."

The Companions said, "Not even you O Messenger of Allah?" He replied:

> "**Not even me**, except if Allah covers me with mercy from Himself and grace."

That is the seal on the whole passage. Ayah 24 credits the deeds; the hadith locates the cause. Deeds are what Allah allowed you to send ahead — but the door is opened by His mercy and His grace, and it is opened that way even for the best of creation ﷺ. And notice that the hadith does not say *stop working*. Its first words are the opposite: work, strive, draw near. It removes self-congratulation, not effort.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a person, and it is careful to ask no more.

**Build the certainty of ayah 20.** The believer's whole account rests on it — not on an idea he found interesting, but on a conviction he was **certain** of, in Ibn Kathir's word, while ordinary life was going on around him. That certainty is what quietly writes the file.

**Confess rather than argue.** In both reports, what precedes the forgiveness is a servant saying *yes, my Lord, I did it* — sins on the outside of the record, admitted, and only then covered. There is a form of honesty with Allah in this life that rehearses that moment now, in private, before it happens in public.

**Send parcels forward on days that feel like nothing.** Ayah 24 calls them the days gone by. They will not feel like the days on which a Paradise is being furnished. They never do. But that is exactly what the ayah says they were — and then leaves you standing under a tree whose fruit bends down to a man lying on his bed, being told to eat and drink at ease, made welcome by a mercy no deed could have bought.

passages.title: The record in the left hand
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat give us the other half of a pair. Just before this, a man was handed his record in his right hand and called out to everyone within earshot, *"Here, take my account book and read it!"* (69:19). Now the camera turns to the man who receives his record in his **left** hand — and every word out of his mouth is a wish that something had not happened. Ibn Kathir titles this passage "The Bad Condition of Whoever is given His Record in His Left Hand," and says simply: these ayat describe the wretched at the moment they are brought before Allah, "and at this time he will be very remorseful."

What holds ayat 25–29 together is that they are a single, unbroken speech. One man, one breath, five sentences — and not one of them is an argument. He does not say the record is wrong. He does not say he was treated unfairly. He only says: *if only.*

## The mirror of ayah 19

The contrast is deliberate, and it is built into the sound of the words. In ayah 19 the successful man says **هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ** — *hā'umu iqra'ū kitābiyah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **hā'umu** literally means "come," but idiomatically it carries the force of the plural command **khudhū**, "take!" So the man given his record in his right hand "will be elated and, looking at the people around him, will say 'Here, take my account book and read it!'"

That is a man who wants an audience. Ayah 25 is the exact photographic negative: **يَا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُوتَ كِتَابِيَهْ** — *"I wish that I had not been given my Record!"* One man passes the book around. The other wishes the book had never been placed in his hand at all.

Notice, too, that both men end their sentences on the same sound — *kitābiyah*. Across ayat 25–29 that ending drums four times: **كِتَابِيَهْ** (my record), **حِسَابِيَهْ** (my reckoning), **مَالِيَهْ** (my wealth), **سُلْطَانِيَهْ** (my authority). Four possessives in a row: *my, my, my, my.* Everything this man ever called his own is named in the same breath — and every one of them has either turned against him or turned to nothing. The grammar of ownership has become the grammar of loss.

## "And that I had never known how my account is" (ayah 26)

Ayah 26 is stranger than it first looks. He does not wish for a better record. He does not wish the accounting had come out differently. He wishes **not to know** — *"and that I had never known how my account is."*

This is the instinct of a man who has already understood that the verdict cannot be changed, so the only relief left to imagine is ignorance. In this world people avoid opening the letter, avoid the test result, avoid the ledger, and tell themselves that not looking is a kind of safety. On that Day the record is placed in the hand. The passage lets us hear what that particular comfort sounds like once it has become permanently unavailable.

## "Would that it had been my end" (ayah 27)

**يَا لَيْتَهَا كَانَتِ الْقَاضِيَةَ** — *"Would that it had been my end!"* He is wishing that the death he already died had been the **final** thing about him: a full stop rather than a doorway.

That is exactly how the early commentators read it. Ibn Kathir reports **Ad-Daḥḥāk** as saying it means "a death which is not followed by any life," and notes that **Muhammad bin Kaʿb**, **Ar-Rabīʿ** and **As-Suddī** said the same. So the wish is not for a second death to end the punishment; it is a wish backwards — that the first death had been the end of him altogether.

Then **Qatādah** adds the line that turns this ayah into a mirror for the living: *"He will hope for death even though in the worldly life it was the most hated thing to him."* Sit with that. The thing he spent his whole life fleeing, denying, refusing to think about — death — becomes, on that Day, the one mercy he begs for and cannot have. His values have not merely been corrected; they have been turned inside out. What he most feared is now what he most wants, and it is out of reach.

There is an implicit teaching about the resurrection here too. He wishes death had been the end precisely because it was not. He is no longer disputing that he was raised; his own mouth now takes it for granted, and all he has left is the wish that it had never happened.

## "My wealth has not availed me" (ayah 28)

**مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ** — *"My wealth has not availed me."* His wealth was the thing he assumed would always be enough: enough to buy his way out, enough to make him self-sufficient, enough that he never had to feel need. Standing there, he announces the failure of that assumption in the past tense.

Ibn Kathir reads ayat 28 and 29 as one thought: *"my wealth and my honor did not protect me from the punishment of Allah and His torment. Now the matter has ended with me alone and I have no helper nor anyone to save me."*

Those last words — **with me alone** — are the point. Wealth is not only money; it is the network money buys. Lawyers, connections, staff, dependants, admirers, the people who take your call. All of that is a kind of insulation, and it works reliably enough in this life that a man can mistake it for protection. Ayah 28 is the moment the insulation is stripped away and he discovers he is, and always was, one solitary soul answerable to his Lord — with, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "no helper nor anyone to save me."

## "My power has gone from me" (ayah 29)

The last sentence of his speech is **هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ** — *"My power has gone from me!"*, or as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, "My power has gone from me for good."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings of **sulṭān**, and both are worth holding.

**First: power.** Literally *sulṭān* "yields the sense of 'power or overpowering'. Therefore, a government or state is referred to as saltanah and a ruler is referred to as sultan." Maʿārif then draws out what such power does to a person: "when people gain power and political ascendancy in the world, they become proud, hold sway over other people, perpetrate injustices and commit atrocities. But in the Hereafter all that will vanish and be lost, and the unjust and proud rulers will have no army to obey or support them. They will be miserable and helpless creatures who will not be able to defend themselves."

Read that against ayah 28 and you see the two pillars of worldly security named in order: **money**, then **muscle**. What you can buy, and what you can command. The tyrant's power was never really his own; it lived in the obedience of other people, and on that Day, in Maʿārif's words, there is "no army to obey or support them."

**Second: proof.** Maʿārif notes that *sulṭān* "also stands for 'authority, proof or argument'," in which case the ayah means: *"Today I have no argument in favour of protecting myself against punishment."* This second sense fits the courtroom setting of the passage exactly. The record has been read; the defendant rises to speak; and what he says is that he has nothing to say. Five sentences of pure wishing, and not one point of defence. Both meanings may well be intended together: the ruler has lost his troops, and the accused has lost his case.

## What answers him

His speech ends at ayah 29, and nobody replies to him. Instead a command is given *about* him, over his head, as though he were no longer a party to the conversation: *"Seize him and fetter him; then throw him in the blazing Fire"* (69:30–31). Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "will command the guardians of Hell to forcibly remove him from the gathering place, fetter him — meaning put iron collars on his neck — then carry him off to Hell and cast him into it."

Notice the precision of the irony. In ayah 29 he complains that his *sulṭān*, his power to command, has gone. The very next thing we hear is a command being carried out — on him. The man who once gave orders becomes the object of one, seized by hands he cannot bargain with. And the collars go onto the neck of a man whose only remaining possessions are the four things he has just listed: a record, a reckoning, a wealth that did nothing, and a power that is gone.

## Living it

A warning is only useful if it reaches us while there is still time to act. Three things this passage asks of us directly.

**Do not put off looking at your record.** His first two wishes (ayat 25–26) are wishes for ignorance. The believer does the opposite now, willingly: he opens his own account while the ledger can still be corrected — takes himself to task, repents, returns what he owes, mends what he broke. Every honest self-reckoning in this life is a page you will not be ambushed by in the next.

**Test what you are relying on.** Ayah 28 is a question in disguise: *what, exactly, do I think will be enough?* Everyone leans on something — savings, a job, a family name, a reputation, a network. None of these are evil in themselves; the danger is the quiet assumption that they constitute safety. Keep Ibn Kathir's phrase close as the corrective: on that Day, *"the matter has ended with me alone."*

**Handle power as a trust, not a possession.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's comment applies to anyone with authority over anyone — a manager, a parent, an official, a person with the power to make someone else's day easier or harder. Power that made you proud and let you wrong people is precisely the power ayah 29 says has gone from him for good. It was never really his. What survives is only how it was used.

And behind all of it stands the claim this man's own mouth confirms: the Reckoning is real, it is coming, and the wish of ayah 27 — *would that it had been my end* — will not be granted. Far better to be the man of ayah 19, holding out his book and saying: *here, take my account book and read it.*

passages.title: The command to seize, and its reasons
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are a single verdict, spoken over the man who was handed his record in his left hand. Ayat 30–32 are the sentence itself — three short commands, seize, burn, bind — and ayat 33–37 are the reasons and the consequences: two things he failed to do in the world, and two things he will not find in the Fire.

What holds the passage together is that shape: **command, then cause.** The Qur'an does not simply describe a punishment; it immediately tells you why, and the "why" is small enough to fit in two lines. That is what makes this passage searching rather than merely frightening.

Ibn Kathir reads these ayat together with the ones just before them: they describe the condition of the wretched when one of them is given his record of deeds in his left hand as the people are brought before Allah, and he is overcome with remorse. By ayah 29 he has named what failed him — his wealth did not avail him, his power has gone from him. Ibn Kathir paraphrases that state of mind: my wealth and my honour did not protect me from Allah's punishment; the matter has now ended with me alone, and I have no helper and no one to save me. It is at that point — a man standing entirely alone — that Ibn Kathir's commentary moves on with the words *At this Allah says*, and ayah 30 begins.

## Ayah 30: "Seize him — then collar him"

**خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ** — *Khudhūhu fa-ghullūhu.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, "Seize him, then put a collar around his neck." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah will command the guardians of Hell to remove him forcibly from the place of gathering, and to *fetter* him — which he glosses precisely: **to put iron collars on his neck.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to read past. The order is issued — but *the wording of the ayah does not mention who will seize him and who will truss him up.* No angel is named, no group identified; it is simply "Seize him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the instruction is given to the angels to seize the guilty one and truss him up by putting a collar around his neck, and adds that narratives indicate that when this order is issued, **everything — like submissive, obedient servants — will rush to apprehend him.**

Sit with the contrast. In ayah 29 the man's own words are *My power has gone from me.* In ayah 30 the whole of creation moves at a single word from Allah.

## Ayah 31: into the Fire

**ثُمَّ ٱلۡجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ** — "then burn them in Hell." Ibn Kathir keeps the sequence tight: they carry him off to Hell and cast him into it — *meaning*, he says, **they will submerge him in it.** Not left at the edge of the Fire, but immersed in it.

## Ayah 32: the chain of seventy cubits

**ثُمَّ فِي سِلۡسِلَةٖ ذَرۡعُهَا سَبۡعُونَ ذِرَاعٗا فَٱسۡلُكُوهُ** — "then tie them up with chains seventy arms long." Ibn Kathir's rendering is "a chain whereof the length is seventy cubits"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same measure as "seventy hands."

But whose measure? Ibn Kathir preserves the answers of the early authorities, and each one stretches the picture further:

- **Ka'b Al-Ahbar:** every ring of it will be equal to the entire amount of iron found in this world.
- **Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj** (reported by Al-'Awfi): each cubit will be **the forearm's length of an angel** — so the measure is not a human yardstick at all.

Then there is the verb itself, *fa-uslukūhu*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the two readings honestly rather than choosing silently. The phrase "make him enter into a chain" **could** be interpreted metaphorically as simply "bind him in a chain"; but it **could** be taken in its primary sense — to pierce the chain through one side of the body so that it comes out from the other side, the way a string is passed through a pearl or the bead of a rosary. Traditional narratives, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, seem to support the primary sense — a point it marks with a citation to Mazharī.

Ibn Kathir's material points the same way. Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the chain will be entered into him and pulled out of his mouth, and that they will then be arranged on it "just like locusts are arranged on a stick that is being roasted." Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas a similar description, ending with the detail that **he will not be able to stand on his two feet.**

The image of the skewered locusts is worth pausing on. It is not only agony — it is *indignity*, and *multitude*. He is one of many, strung along a chain. The man whose wealth and honour Ibn Kathir describes has become an item on a line.

## From the Sunnah: how far the chain reaches

Ibn Kathir records that **Imam Ahmad** narrated from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that if a drop of lead like this — and he pointed to a skull bone — were sent from the heaven to the earth, a distance of five hundred years' travel, it would reach the earth before night; and if that same drop were sent from the *head of the chain* of Hell, it would travel forty fall seasons, night and day, before it would reach Hell's cavity or its base. Ibn Kathir notes that **At-Tirmidhi** also recorded this hadith, and that At-Tirmidhi said: "This Hadith is Hasan."

The hadith is not a riddle about physics. It measures a depth the mind cannot hold, and it does so by first giving you something you *can* picture — a falling weight, a single day — and then breaking the scale.

## Ayat 33–34: the two reasons

Everything above answers *what*. These two ayat answer *why*, and they are the heart of the passage:

**إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ لَا يُؤۡمِنُ بِٱللَّهِ ٱلۡعَظِيمِ** — "Verily, he **used not to** believe in Allah, the Most Great."

**وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلۡمِسۡكِينِ** — "and **urged not** the feeding of the poor."

Note that Allah is named here with the attribute **al-ʿAẓīm, the Most Great**: the greatness he refused to acknowledge is stated in the very sentence that condemns him.

Ibn Kathir reads the pair as the two rights a person owes. He did not establish **the right of Allah** upon him — of obedience to Him and performing His worship; and he did not benefit **Allah's creation**, nor did he give them their rights.

He then states the principle plainly: Allah has a right upon the servants that they worship Him alone and not associate anything with Him; and the servants of Allah have a right upon each other to good treatment and assistance in righteousness and piety. **For this reason,** Ibn Kathir says, Allah commanded performance of the prayer and the payment of Zakah — one duty facing upward, one facing outward.

He brings a moving witness to how central these two remained to the very end: when the Prophet ﷺ was in his last moments, near death, he said, *"The prayer, and your right hand possessions."* (Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ words here without naming a collection.) Even as life left him, the two things he pressed upon the community were his Lord's right and the right of the most vulnerable people in their care.

Now look again at ayah 34 and notice where the charge stops. It is not that he did not feed the poor; it is that he **did not urge** it. He is not condemned merely for closing his own hand, but for never even prompting anyone else to open theirs. And the object of the neglect is *ṭaʿām al-miskīn* — the needy person's *food*. Not his comfort, not his advancement: his meal.

## Ayat 35–36: no friend, and nothing to eat

The punishment now answers the crime, item for item.

**فَلَيۡسَ لَهُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ هَٰهُنَا حَمِيمٞ** — "So this Day they will have no close friend here." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines *ḥamīm* as **"a sincere or bosom friend."** Ibn Kathir expands the ayah: there is no one that Day who can save him from the punishment of Allah, nor any close friend, **nor any intercessor whose request would be honoured.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: on the Day of Resurrection he will have no friend that will support him or save him from punishment.

And then the food. **وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنۡ غِسۡلِينٖ** — "nor any food except from *ghislīn*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ghislīn*, with a kasrah (an "i" vowel) on the *gh*, refers to **the water with which the pus and blood of the wounds of the inmates of Hell will be washed.** The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites describe it in different but converging ways:

- **Qatadah:** it will be the worst food of the people of the Hellfire.
- **Ar-Rabi' and Ad-Dahhak:** *ghislīn* is a tree in Hell.
- **Ibn 'Abbas** (via 'Ikrimah, reported by Shabib bin Bishr): it will be the blood and fluid that will flow from their flesh.
- **Ibn 'Abbas** (reported by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah): it is the pus of the people of the Hellfire.

The man who would not urge that a poor person be given a meal is left with this for a meal. The correspondence is exact, and it is the passage's own argument.

**A question the scholars addressed.** If ayah 36 says he has "no food except *ghislīn*," how does that sit with the Qur'an's statement elsewhere that the inmates of Hell will eat *zaqqūm*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the words "nor any food" mean they will not have any **delectable food** to eat. That statement does not negate things like *ghislīn*, which are distasteful and reprehensible; therefore it does not contradict the ayah about *zaqqūm*.

## Ayah 37: who eats it

**لَّا يَأۡكُلُهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱلۡخَٰطِـُٔونَ** — "which none will eat except the evildoers" — the word left in the Arabic by Ibn Kathir as *al-Khāṭi'ūn*, and rendered in the translation as "the evildoers."

Neither Ibn Kathir nor Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops to define the word further here, and the passage itself has just named the failings at issue: not believing in Allah, the Most Great, and not urging the feeding of the poor. The final ayah closes the circle, and the word "except" makes it a boundary as much as a verdict: **this is nobody's meal but theirs.**

## Living it

Read the way Ibn Kathir reads it, this passage is not a catalogue of horrors for its own sake. It is a diagnostic laid over an ordinary life.

- **Two rights, not one.** Ibn Kathir's framing is the practical takeaway: Allah's right upon His servants — that they worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him — and the servants' right upon each other, which he defines as good treatment and assistance in righteousness and piety. This man failed at both, and Ibn Kathir points out that this is exactly why the prayer and Zakah were commanded.
- **Encouragement counts.** Ayah 34 names *urging* the feeding of the poor as a thing whose absence is held against him. Raising the subject, organising the meal, reminding a friend, giving the cause a nudge — if the failure to do even this appears in the charge, then doing it is worth something.
- **Assets do not travel.** Wealth and power are what this man cites in his own words, and Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is blunt: they did not protect him from the punishment of Allah, and the matter ended with him alone, with no helper and no one to save him.
- **Nor do connections.** Ibn Kathir specifies that on that Day there is no close friend and *no intercessor whose request would be honoured*. The habit of relying on who you know has an expiry date.

And there is mercy folded into the frightening length of that chain. Every one of these ayat was revealed to be heard *now*, by people who still have their wealth in their hands, their friends within reach, and a hungry person somewhere near enough to feed.

passages.title: An oath: the Qur'an is not a poet's word
passages.tafsir:
As the sūrah closes, it turns to the question lying underneath everything that came before it: **where did this recitation come from?** Ayat 38–43 answer with an oath sworn on the whole of existence — everything you can see and everything you cannot — and then with a chain of denials and one final, settled statement: this is a revelation sent down from the Lord of all the worlds.

What holds the six ayat together is a single argument built in three moves. First the oath (38–39). Then the claim the oath is sworn to uphold: it is the word of an honoured Messenger (40). Then the clearing away of two descriptions the ayat themselves name and refuse — poet, soothsayer (41–42) — before ayah 43 names the true source.

## The oath: everything seen and everything unseen

Ibn Kathir explains the structure plainly. **Allah swears by His creation**, in which some of His signs can be seen in His creatures — and these signs, he adds, "indicate the perfection of His Names and Attributes." Then He swears by **the hidden things that they cannot see**. Between the two halves of the oath, nothing is left out.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about scope: the pairing "what you see and what you do not see" **comprehends the entire body of creation**. It then records two interpretations from the commentator Mazharī of what specifically "what you do not see" points to:

- **Some say** it refers to the Being of Allah Taʿālā and His attributes.
- **Others say** "what you see" refers to the things of this mortal world, and "what you do not see" refers to the things of the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not settle between them, closing with the scholars' habitual reserve: *And Allah, the Pure and Exalted, Knows best.* That reserve is worth imitating. The two readings are not enemies. Either way, the sweep of the oath is total — and either way, the unseen is being sworn by exactly as the visible is.

That is worth pausing over. The oath does not confine itself to what can be pointed at. To the One swearing, the seen and the unseen are alike His creation and alike available to be sworn by — which is itself an answer to anyone who treats what lies beyond sight as though it were beyond truth.

## "The word of an honoured Messenger" (ayah 40)

Here is where a careful reader can go wrong, and where Ibn Kathir is most valuable.

إِنَّهُۥ لَقَوۡلُ رَسُولٖ كَرِيمٖ — *"That this is verily the word of an honoured Messenger."*

Taken alone, that could sound as if the Qur'an is the Messenger's own composition. It is not, and the passage itself will say so two ayat later. Ibn Kathir explains **why the word "Messenger" is exactly the right word to use**:

> "Allah gave this description to him, a description which carries the meaning of **conveying**, because the duty of a messenger is to convey from the sender."

That is the whole key. A *rasūl* — a messenger, an envoy — is by definition someone carrying speech that originated with someone else. To call the Qur'an "the word of a Messenger" is to say: it reaches you **through** him, on the authority of the One who sent him. The title itself refuses the idea of authorship.

**Who is the Messenger in ayah 40?** Ibn Kathir says: **Muhammad ﷺ**. And then he does something illuminating — he sets this ayah beside its near-twin in Sūrat at-Takwīr, where the identical phrase appears:

> إِنَّهُۥ لَقَوۡلُ رَسُولٖ كَرِيمٍ — ذِى قُوَّةٍ عِندَ ذِى ٱلۡعَرۡشِ مَكِينٖ — مُّطَاعٖ ثَمَّ أَمِينٖ
> *"Verily, this is the Word of (this Qur'an brought by) a most honourable messenger. Owner of power (and high rank) with Allah, the Lord of the Throne. Obeyed and trustworthy."* (81:19–21)

There, Ibn Kathir says, **the "honoured messenger" refers to Jibrīl** — described as owner of power and high rank with Allah, the Lord of the Throne, and as "obeyed and trustworthy." That sūrah then goes on: *"and your companion is not a madman"* (81:22) — which, Ibn Kathir says, means Muhammad ﷺ; *"And indeed he saw him in the clear horizon"* (81:23) — meaning Muhammad ﷺ **saw Jibrīl in his true form, the form in which Allah created him**; *"And he is not ḍanīn with the Unseen"* (81:24) — which Ibn Kathir glosses as **suspicious**; and *"And it is not the word of the outcast Shayṭān"* (81:25) — which he says is similar to what is being said in our passage.

Ibn Kathir then draws the conclusion that ties the two sūrahs together:

> "So in one instance Allah applies the term *messenger* to the angelic Messenger and in another instance He applies it to the human Messenger (Muhammad ﷺ). This is because **both of them are conveying from Allah that which has been entrusted to them of Allah's revelation and Speech**."

So the same title fits both, for the same reason. The Qur'an travelled a route: from Allah, to Jibrīl, to Muhammad ﷺ, to those who received it — and at every stage it stayed what it was, because at every stage the one carrying it was carrying, not composing. This is why Ibn Kathir titles the whole passage **"The Qur'an is the Speech of Allah"**: the oath, he says, is "an oath swearing that the Qur'an is His Speech, His inspiration and His revelation to His servant and Messenger, whom He chose to convey His Message, and the Messenger carried out this trust faithfully."

## The two denials, and the two rebukes (ayat 41–42)

Now the passage clears the ground. Two descriptions are named and refused:

**"It is not the word of a poet"** (ayah 41) — وَمَا هُوَ بِقَوۡلِ شَاعِرٖ.

**"Nor is it the word of a soothsayer"** (ayah 42) — وَلَا بِقَوۡلِ كَاهِنٖ. The word *kāhin* is rendered in the translations before us as *soothsayer*, and in another as *fortune-teller*.

Notice that both denials use the same construction as ayah 40: *qawl*, "the word/speech of…". The passage is not arguing about literary quality; it is arguing about **origin**. Whose speech is this? The answer given is not "a poet's", and not "a soothsayer's" — and in the parallel Ibn Kathir cites from at-Takwīr, not "the outcast Shayṭān's" either. The candidates are struck off one by one, until ayah 43 names the true source.

**The two rebukes are not interchangeable.** Each denial is followed by a different reproach, and the pairing repays attention:

- After *poet*: **قَلِيلٗا مَّا تُؤۡمِنُونَ** — "little is that you **believe**" / "you hardly believe."
- After *soothsayer*: **قَلِيلٗا مَّا تَذَكَّرُونَ** — "little is that you **remember**" / "you are hardly mindful."

The first names what is missing as *īmān*, faith — the trusting acceptance the Qur'an asks for. The second names it as *tadhakkur*, remembering, taking heed, calling to mind what you already know. And both are addressed directly to "you", not to some distant third party.

There is also a sting in the smallness of the word *qalīlan*, "little". It does not say *you never believe* or *you never remember*. It says: **very little**. That is a more uncomfortable diagnosis than outright denial, because it fits people who do believe a bit and reflect occasionally — who hear the recitation and then live as though they had not. Read that way, the address is not sealed off in the past. It lands on any listener whose belief and whose remembering are thinner than what stands in front of them deserves.

## "A revelation from the Lord of all the worlds" (ayah 43)

تَنزِيلٞ مِّن رَّبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ — Ibn Kathir renders it, *"This is the revelation sent down from the Lord of all that exists."*
