The passage has been building to exactly this. The oath in 38–39 swept up the seen and the unseen; the two denials in 41–42 cleared away the false attributions; and now the true source is named — and named with the title **Rabb al-ʿālamīn**, the Lord of *all* the worlds, of all that exists. The One who owns everything the oath was sworn by is the One this recitation came down from. The word *tanzīl*, rendered here as "the revelation **sent down**", carries that direction in it: from Him to us. Nothing in it rose up from the earth.

Ibn Kathir's summary of the whole movement is worth holding onto: this is "an oath swearing that the Qur'an is His Speech, His inspiration and His revelation to His servant and Messenger, whom He chose to convey His Message, and the Messenger carried out this trust faithfully."

## Living with these ayat

**Treat the unseen as real.** Allah swore by what you cannot see alongside what you can. Whether that unseen is understood, as Mazharī's two reports have it, as His own Being and attributes or as the realities of the Hereafter, the lesson for the one reciting is the same: a life ordered only around the visible is a life ordered around half of what exists.

**Receive the Qur'an as speech, from a Speaker.** Ibn Kathir's heading is not decoration — "The Qur'an is the Speech of Allah." Ayat 40 and 43 together mean that when you open the muṣḥaf you are not reading *about* Allah; you are receiving words He sent down. That should change the posture of the reader before it changes anything else.

**Honour the trust that carried it to you.** The chain in Ibn Kathir's reading — Allah, then Jibrīl "obeyed and trustworthy", then Muhammad ﷺ who "carried out this trust faithfully" — is a chain of *amānah*, faithful custody. Each carrier conveyed what was entrusted to him, and conveyed it whole. That is why what reaches you is what was sent.

**Ask honestly which rebuke fits you.** The passage does not accuse its hearers of having no faith and no memory. It accuses them of having **little** — قَلِيلٗا. The believer's use of ayat 41–42 is not to point at others but to ask: is my belief proportionate to what I claim to accept, and how often do I actually call it to mind? And Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.

passages.title: If the Messenger had invented revelation
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat bring the argument of Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah to its sharpest point with a single, breathtaking sentence: *if* the Messenger ﷺ had made up even some statements in Allah's Name, Allah would have seized him and severed his life-artery, and not one of you could have shielded him. It is a defence of the truth of the Qur'an made by describing — in the most violent terms — what would have happened to the Prophet ﷺ had the accusers been right.

## The accusation being answered

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: the disbelievers used to accuse the Prophet ﷺ of being a poet and a soothsayer, and to say that the Qur'an was the word of a poet or the word of a soothsayer. The Qur'an denounces that argument: it is not the word of a poet nor the word of a soothsayer; it is a revelation from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ. Earlier in the sūrah, in ayat 37–38, the case had already been put that all visible and invisible things prove that the Prophet ﷺ is Allah's true Messenger and that the Qur'an is Allah's revealed Word — "not the imaginary flight of a poet's mind or the wild conjectures of a diviner."

Now, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, in these verses "another invincible argument is given in support of his claim." The accusers had claimed the Prophet ﷺ was inventing this and attributing it to Allah. Very well — follow that claim to its end and see what it would have meant.

## An argument built on an impossible "if"

Ayah 44 is built on a supposition that neither commentary treats as a real possibility. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the argument "is put forward in a strong language — assuming the impossible — to make the ignorant realise the worst-case scenario." Ibn Kathir spells the unspoken half out for us: "if Muḥammad forged something against Us, **as they claim** … then We would surely be swift in punishing him. And of course, Muḥammad did not do any of this."

The key verb is **taqawwala**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its sense plainly: *taqawwul* means "to forge, fabricate or concoct." It is not simply "to say"; it is to manufacture speech and then pin it on someone else. And the object is **baʿḍ al-aqāwīl** — rendered by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "some statements," not *all* of them.

Notice how little would have been required. Ibn Kathir unpacks exactly what would have counted: if he "added or removed anything from the Message, or said anything from himself while attributing it to Us." Adding, removing, or speaking from himself — any one of the three, in Allah's Name.

And notice where the forgery is aimed. Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "forged a false saying **concerning Us**"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "forged some statements **in Our name**." The crime named here is not lying in general. It is speaking in Allah's Name what Allah did not say. That is what would have cost him his life.

## "We would have seized him by the right hand"

Ayah 45 begins the sentence of execution, and the first thing that happens is a grip.

Ibn Kathir reports, without naming its source, an explanation of the phrase: "It has been said that this means, 'We would seize him by the right hand because it is more stronger in grabbing.'" On this reading the strong hand is taken first — the hand that would resist.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a different picture, and offers it tentatively — the expression 'right hand' is used, it says, *probably* because of the scene of a public execution: "when a convicted criminal is to be executed, the executioner stands in front facing the condemned person. The executioner's left hand faces the guilty person's right hand. The executioner holds the condemned person with his left hand and attacks him with his right hand." In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary of the argument, "Allah's strong hand would have seized him by the throat and cut off his life-artery and he would have certainly met with a violent death."

The two commentaries fill in the picture differently. What neither leaves in doubt is the image itself: a seizing that cannot be shaken off, followed at once by the blow. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's executioner is offered as an illustration drawn from human experience to make the verse land — not as a description of Allah, who is not a man standing in front of another man.

## "Then We would have severed his aorta"

Ayah 46 names the target: **al-watīn**.

Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbās said it "refers to the artery of the heart, and it is the vein that is attached to the heart," and that the same was said by ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Al-Hakim, Qatādah, Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muslim Al-Baṭin and Abū Ṣakhr Ḥumayd bin Ziyād — a remarkable agreement among the early authorities. Muḥammad bin Kaʿb gave a slightly wider sense: "It is the heart, its blood, and whatever is near it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in the language of the body as we know it: *watīn* refers to "aorta or life-artery," the main artery that carries blood from the heart to other parts of the body — "once this artery is cut off, death occurs instantly."

Feel the precision of the choice. The verse does not say "We would have killed him," nor "We would have destroyed his people," nor "We would have disgraced him." It names one vessel, the single line on which a human life hangs. And the ayah says *then*: the seizing, then the cut. Two movements, in order, unhurried. Sentence, then execution. There is nothing vague in this threat, and nothing survivable in it.

## "And none of you could have shielded him"

Ayah 47 turns from the Prophet ﷺ to the audience and closes the last exit. Ibn Kathir explains: "none of you would be able to come between Us and him if We wanted to do any of this to him."

Note the addressee. It is not "none of *them*" but *none of **you*** — the ayah speaks directly to the very people who were making the accusation. Whatever protection they might imagine standing between this man and consequences, the verse removes it in advance: no one comes between Allah and the one Allah intends to seize.

## What the argument actually establishes

Ibn Kathir gathers the whole passage into one conclusion: "The meaning behind all of this is to say that he ﷺ is truthful, righteous and guided because Allah determined what he is to convey from Him, and Allah helps him with fantastic miracles and definite proofs."

So the passage is doing two things at once. It vindicates the Prophet ﷺ, and at the same time it makes clear that he is not the author. A forger protects his own words; here the Speaker declares He would have protected His words *from* the one who carries them. The Messenger ﷺ has no editorial rights over the message — Allah, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "determined what he is to convey from Him." That is precisely what "revelation" means, and it is why these ayat, though phrased as a threat, stand among the strongest testimonies to his honour.

## A cautionary note

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important caution, and it is worth stating carefully. This verse "refers to a theoretical situation relating to the Apostle of Allah in particular that lest — Allah forbid — if he were to concoct a word and impute it to Allah, this is the way he would have been dealt with. A hypothetical situation is a possible situation, not an actual situation."

And, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues, "this does not necessarily set down a universal principle that any and every impostor, who lays claim to prophethood, would be destroyed as a matter of general rule. History records that many impostors laid claim to prophethood, but no such destructive punishment was ever imposed on them." The verse is a statement about how Allah would have dealt with His own Messenger ﷺ in particular — not a test we may run on claimants by watching whether they drop dead.

## Living it

The passage is aimed at the accusers, but it leaves a weight on every believer who speaks about religion.

**Speaking in Allah's Name is the most dangerous speech there is.** If the man Allah chose was told what would have followed the forging of even "some statements" in Allah's Name, what is our position when we say "Allah says," or "Islam says," or "this is halal, that is haram," on nothing but a half-memory or a feeling? Ibn Kathir's phrasing is the standard to measure against: adding, removing, or saying something from oneself while attributing it to Allah. The honest "I don't know" is not weakness. It is the only safe ground.

**Take the Qur'an as it was given.** The integrity this passage guards at the source is asked of us in the receiving. If the Messenger ﷺ had no licence to add to it, remove from it, or slip in a word of his own, we have no licence to select the ayat that suit us and quietly set aside the ones that do not.

**And take confidence from it.** These ayat were put before people who were accusing the Prophet ﷺ of exactly this — and the Book they doubted turned on its own carrier in front of them and put his life on the line. That is not how a fabrication behaves. As Ibn Kathir concludes, this is a man who is "truthful, righteous and guided," and the words he brought are what they claim to be.

These five ayat close Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah. Having just silenced the accusation that the Qur'an was the Prophet's ﷺ own invention, Allah now turns to what this Book actually *is* — a reminder, a coming regret, and certain truth — and then gives the Prophet ﷺ a single instruction to carry it all: glorify your Lord.

What holds the passage together is one repeated word: **innahu** — "and indeed it is." Three times over (ayah 48, ayah 50, ayah 51) Allah makes a statement about the same "it," and Ibn Kathir identifies that "it" as the Qur'an. The Book is named three times from three angles — what it is for those who have taqwā, what it becomes for the denier, and what it is in itself — and then ayah 52 tells the one who received it what to do.

## The argument that has just been made

To feel the force of ayah 48, you have to hear what comes immediately before it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the setting: the disbelievers used to accuse the Prophet ﷺ of being a poet and a soothsayer, and said the Qur'an was the word of a poet or the word of a soothsayer. Ayat 37–38 had already argued that everything visible and invisible proves that he is Allah's true Messenger and that the Qur'an is Allah's revealed Word — not the imaginary flight of a poet's mind nor the wild conjectures of a diviner.

Then, in ayat 44–47, comes what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls another invincible argument. *And had he forged some statements in Our name, We would have certainly seized him by the right hand, and then severed his life-artery.* The word **taqawwul**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means "to forge, fabricate or concoct." **Al-watīn** refers to the aorta or life-artery — the main artery that carries blood from the heart to the other parts of the body; once it is cut off, death occurs instantly. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that al-watīn "refers to the artery of the heart, and it is the vein that is attached to the heart" — a view also transmitted from ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥākim, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muslim al-Baṭīn and Abū Ṣakhr Ḥumayd ibn Ziyād. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb said it is "the heart, its blood, and whatever is near it."

Ibn Kathir summarises the logic: if Muhammad ﷺ had forged something against Allah as they claim — adding to the Message, removing from it, or saying anything of his own while attributing it to Allah — Allah would surely have been swift in punishing him; and none of them could have come between Allah and him. And of course he ﷺ did none of this. The meaning behind all of it, Ibn Kathir says, is that he ﷺ is truthful, righteous and guided, because Allah determined what he was to convey and helps him with fantastic miracles and definite proofs.

**A cautionary note.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important qualification here. This is a theoretical situation relating to the Messenger ﷺ in particular — put forward in deliberately strong language, assuming the impossible, to make the ignorant realise the worst-case scenario. A hypothetical situation is a possible situation, not an actual one. It does not necessarily lay down a universal principle that any and every impostor claiming prophethood would be destroyed as a general rule; history records that many impostors laid claim to prophethood and no such destructive punishment was ever imposed on them.

So when ayah 48 begins, the ground has been cleared. The Book is not his invention. Now: what is it?

## Ayah 48 — "a reminder for those who have taqwā"

*And indeed, this Qur'an is a reminder to those mindful of Allah.*

Notice who is named. It is a reminder **li'l-muttaqīn** — rendered in the sources as "those mindful of Allah," "those who have Taqwa," and "those conscious of Allah."

Ibn Kathir explains that the "it" is the Qur'an, and pairs this ayah with another: *Say: "It is for those who believe, a guide and a healing. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness (deafness) in their ears, and it is blindness for them"* (41:44). The same recitation falls on two sets of ears. To one it is guidance and a cure; to the other it is thickness in the hearing and darkness over the eyes.

This is the passage's quiet challenge. The Book itself is settled — ayah 51 will call it absolute truth. What differs, on the evidence of 41:44, is the one receiving it. A reminder only works on someone willing to be reminded. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: the Divine Word is a reminder and an admonition for those conscious of Allah.

## Ayah 49 — "and We certainly know"

*And We certainly know that some of you will persist in denial.*

Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and it lands hard: **with this explanation and clarification, there will still be among you those who reject the Qur'an.** The argument has been laid out. The proof has been given. The Book has been vindicated. And Allah says — before anyone can pretend otherwise — that He knows some will still say no.

Two things are worth sitting with here.

First, the honesty. The passage does not promise that clear evidence produces universal belief. It states the opposite in advance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān phrases it this way: Allah knows that despite knowing the absolutely incontestable truth, many people will continue to reject it. Denial, then, is not simply a failure of information.

Second, the comfort. This ayah comes directly before Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ what to do (ayah 52), and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that command as a response to his distress at what they say. The rejection he is meeting is something Allah already knew and already told him about. **"We certainly know"** is not aimed at the deniers only; it steadies the one carrying the message.

Note also the phrasing Ibn Kathir gives: *there are some among you that deny*. Some — not all. The audience is addressed as a whole, and within it a portion is identified.

## Ayah 50 — the regret

*And it will surely be a source of regret for the disbelievers.*

**Ḥasrah** is rendered in the sources as anguish and regret — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it a source of eternal remorse, disappointment and punishment in the Hereafter for the disbelievers. This is not ordinary sadness. It is the grief of someone who realises, too late, exactly what he had in his hands and pushed away.

**Two readings of "it."** Ibn Kathir transmits both:

- **Ibn Jarīr** said: *"And verily this rejection will be anguish for the disbelievers on the Day of Judgement."* On this reading, what torments them is their own denial — the choice itself, seen clearly at last. Ibn Kathir adds that Ibn Jarīr also mentioned a similar statement from Qatādah.
- **Alternatively**, Ibn Kathir says, it is possible that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, in which case the ayah would mean that the Qur'an and belief in it are a cause of anguish for the disbelievers.

Ibn Kathir supports this second possibility with two ayat that show something placed permanently out of reach: *Thus have We caused it to enter the hearts of the criminals. They will not believe in it* (26:200–201), and *And a barrier will be set between them and that which they desire* (34:54). The picture is of a door closing. On the Day when they finally want what belief offers, a barrier stands between them and it — and the very Book that was offered to them becomes the sharpest edge of their regret.

Read the two readings together and the passage has an unbroken arc: the same Book that is a **reminder** in ayah 48 is a **regret** in ayah 50. Nothing about the Book changed.

## Ayah 51 — the truth of certainty

*And indeed, this Qur'an is the absolute truth.*

Ibn Kathir explains **ḥaqq al-yaqīn** as the right and truthful news **in which there is no doubt, suspicion or confusion.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: the Qur'an is undeniably the Truth of Certainty; there is no room for any doubt or suspicion in it.

This is the settling of the whole sūrah's argument. Ayah 49 acknowledged that people will deny; ayah 51 states the status of the Book regardless. Truth is not decided by how many accept it. And placing this statement *after* the acknowledgement of denial is telling: first the honest admission, then the unshaken verdict.

## Ayah 52 — "So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most Great"

*So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest.*

Everything has been building to this **fa-** — "so," "therefore." Given that the Book is a reminder, given that some will deny, given that denial will end in regret, given that this is certain truth — *therefore*: **fa-sabbiḥ**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the command as: "So, pronounce the purity of the name of your magnificent Lord." Ibn Kathir's note on *your Lord, the Most Great* is beautifully economical: this is **"He Who sent down this magnificent Qur'an."** The greatness being glorified is the greatness of the One whose speech has just been defended.

**Why this command, at this moment?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the pastoral point. The Prophet ﷺ should not pay any heed to the criticisms of the obdurate disbelievers, nor should he feel distressed. He should rather pronounce the purity of Allah's name — and this will relieve his distress and grief. It cites the parallel elsewhere in the Qur'an: *And We know that your heart feels distressed for what they say. So, proclaim the purity and glory of your Lord and be among those who prostrate* (15:97–98). The prescription is identical. The best remedy for his distress and grief, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is to glorify Allah, praise Him and prostrate before Him.

Notice what Allah does *not* tell him to do. Not argue harder. Not win the crowd. Not take the insult personally. The response to being disbelieved is to turn toward Allah and declare the purity of His name.

## From the Sunnah — where this ayah lives in your prayer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that **Abu Dawud** records a narration from Sayyidnā ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir Juhanī (may Allah be pleased with him): when the ayah *So, pronounce the purity of the name of your magnificent Lord* (69:52) was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ instructed that this tasbīḥ be reserved for the posture of **rukūʿ**; and when *Pronounce the purity of the name of your most Exalted Lord* (87:1) was revealed, he instructed that that tasbīḥ be reserved for the posture of **sajdah**.

This is the origin of the words on your tongue several times a day when you bow and when you go down in prostration. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that by common consent of the Ummah these tasbīḥāt are recited in rukūʿ and sajdah respectively; according to the overwhelming majority it is Sunnah to recite them and to repeat them three times, while some scholars say it is obligatory.

That is a striking thing to realise at the end of a sūrah about the Day of Reality. The command that closes al-Ḥāqqah was not left as a general sentiment. The Prophet ﷺ took it and fixed it into the posture of bowing, so that the answer to denial, distress, and the whole weight of this passage is something a believer performs, in his body, every single day.

## Living it

**When the Book does not move you, examine yourself, not the Book.** Ayah 48 and ayah 51 together are decisive: the Qur'an is truth in which there is no doubt, and it is a reminder for those who have taqwā. If a recitation passes over you without effect, the ayah points inward — toward the 41:44 diagnosis Ibn Kathir cites: heaviness in the ears, rather than a defect in what is being said.

**Do not measure the message by how many accept it.** Ayah 49 removed that measure in advance. With the explanation and clarification complete, Allah says, there will still be those who reject.

**Take the regret of ayah 50 seriously now, while it can still be acted on.** Ḥasrah, as the sources describe it, is remorse in the Hereafter. Hearing about it in this life is the mercy in the warning.

**And when people speak against what you hold sacred, and it wounds you** — the Prophet ﷺ was given the answer in ayah 52. Not retaliation, not despair, and not a defence of Allah's honour as though it were in danger. Just: pronounce the purity of the name of your Lord, the Most Great. Say it in your rukūʿ tomorrow morning knowing where it came from, and this sūrah about the Day of Reality ends where it should — with your forehead heading toward the ground.

*This is the end of the explanation of Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah. And to Allah belong all praise and blessings.*
